To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the two original tumor cell strains and a lymphoblastoid transformed cell line are highly invasive in vitro, whereas two established transformed cell lines and two primary human cell strains are not.

the two original tumor cell strains, HeLa and AFi, showed aggressive growth and invaded the decidual tissue, whereas the two transformed cell lines HeLa S3, FL, and Girardi Heart and the freshly explanted fetal lung tissue and endometrial tissue did not show aggressive growth and did not invade.
the aggressiveness of tumor cells is not necessarily associated with the degree of transformation of the cell lines.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the invasive properties of human cell lines in confrontation with human decidual tissue and with the possibility of using decidua gravidititis as an in vitro model of tumor invasion
the demonstration that invasive growth is not a property of all transformed cells and that the invasive growth pattern in vitro is not necessarily related to the histological type of the cell line.

the demonstration of a new method for studying invasive growth in vitro, and we have noted differences in the behavior of established cell lines and of primary human explants in confrontation with human decidua graviditisis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the degree of aggressiveness in vitro correlates with the degree of malignancy of the cells.
only cells that are regarded as transformed, either spontaneously or by chemical or viral means, are invasive.
the aggressiveness of a cell line or of a primary explant in the receptor tissue is not necessarily related to its origin or to the presence or absence of malignant transformation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the degree of aggressiveness in vitro is related to the degree of malignancy of the cell lines.
only the two original tumor cell strains, HeLa and AFi, and the lymphoblastoid line showed invasive growth in vitro when confronted with human decidua.
the degree of aggressiveness of the cell lines and explants correlates with their in vivo growth pattern.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the invasive growth of human cells is dependent on the receptor tissue, i.e., the decidua in our case.

invasive growth of cells in vitro can be used as a model for in vitro studies of tumor cell invasion and for the study of interactions between normal cells and the extracellular matrix of the host tissue.
human cells can be classified into three groups: (1) aggressive cells (invasive), (2) nonaggressive cells (noninvasive), and (3) nonaggressive but not invasive (noninvasive) cells.
